canonical_statement: The network evaluated 90 active regimens: 68 NSAID regimens, 19 opioid regimens, and three paracetamol regimens.
Celecoxib 200 mg/day was the most frequently studied active regimen, evaluated in 44 trials.
Commercial funding was reported for 80% of trials and was unclear for 19%.
Allocation concealment was judged at low risk of bias in 15% of trials.
Incomplete pain and physical-function outcome data were judged at low risk of bias in 25% and 26% of trials, respectively.
At six weeks, 38 of 51 oral NSAID, three of nine topical NSAID, four of 18 opioid, and one of three paracetamol regimens were statistically superior to oral placebo for pain.
Seven treatment comparisons had at least a 95% probability of a pain effect exceeding the minimum clinically important difference.
Five oral regimens—diclofenac 150 mg/day, etoricoxib 60 and 90 mg/day, and rofecoxib 25 and 50 mg/day—had at least a 99% probability of exceeding the pain MID.
Topical diclofenac 70-81 and 140-160 mg/day had at least a 92.3% probability of exceeding the pain MID.
Every opioid regimen had a probability of 53% or less of exceeding the pain MID.
Dose-response relations were statistically evident for celecoxib, etoricoxib, naproxcinod, and tramadol.
Treatment effects were similar from one to 12 weeks, and risk-of-bias interactions were not robust.
For physical function, all evaluated interventions improved function versus oral placebo except nabumetone 1000 mg/day and paracetamol below 2000 mg/day.
Evidence of increased dropout due to adverse events was found for 10 of 54 oral NSAID, none of eight topical NSAID, 15 of 18 opioid, and one of three paracetamol regimens.
